claim: Israel was imposed on the land by outside powers, and the Jews took the land by force in 1948.

heard.who: Rashid Khalidi, historian, in a 2024 interview
heard.quote: pushing through the partition resolution, which is the birth certificate of the state of Israel, the 1947 General Assembly resolution, partitioning Palestine

answer: The idea of splitting Palestine came first from a British commission in 1937. Arab leaders rejected it; Jewish opinion was divided. On 29 November 1947 the UN General Assembly recommended a Jewish state and an Arab state, by 33 votes to 13. The Jewish Agency accepted. Palestinian Arab leaders rejected it; the Arab states in the Assembly voted against it, and Saudi Arabia said it did not consider itself bound. Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948, and armies from Arab states entered Palestine on 15 May. By the 1949 ceasefires Israel held more land than the plan had given it, about 78 percent of the former mandate. The record shows a recommendation, one side that accepted it, one that rejected it, and a war.

contested: Khalidi calls the resolution the birth certificate of Israel and says the US and USSR pushed it through; supporters of the vote say it was the best option available and that Jews, many of them Holocaust survivors, also had a claim. Whether Britain, the US and the USSR 'imposed' it or the General Assembly decided it is a question of how one reads great-power influence; this card gives the vote and the rejection and leaves the word 'imposed' to the reader.
The Zionist Congress of 1937 rejected the Peel borders but did not reject partition in principle; the UN secretariat paper says only that both sides rejected it. Sources summarise it differently.

The roughly 78 percent figure and the 56 percent allotted to the Jewish state are measured on different bases, and the figure depends on how the Negev is counted. Sources round differently (Fanack and Explaining History say 78; Encyclopedia.com gives 5,400 to 8,000 square miles); no cited page gives 77. The rest of the former mandate did not go to a Palestinian state: Fanack and the State Department page say Jordan kept the West Bank and East Jerusalem and Egypt took Gaza.
Who started the violence after the November 1947 vote is argued by both sides.

Saudi Arabia's statement to the Assembly on the day of the vote, on the UN page cited in fact 5, says 'pressure' was 'exerted on various representatives' by 'some of the big powers'. This is a statement by an interested government, not a finding.

The State Department page cited in fact 7 says Transjordan's forces intervened 'only in areas that had been designated as part of the arab state' under the plan and the Jerusalem zone. The Arab states gave their aim as preventing partition (Explaining History); Israel and its supporters call the entry an invasion.

On the 1937 Zionist Congress, the Jerusalem Post (citing Walter Laqueur) says Weizmann and Ben-Gurion argued for accepting the plan 'with reservations' and the vote in favour was 300 to 158, so the divide was real but the majority was for negotiating.
could_not_verify: The text of the Peel report itself: the pages I tried (Avalon) did not load. Peel is cited only through reference works and a UN secretariat paper.
The Zionist Congress 1937 decision is stated plainly only by the Jewish Virtual Library (advocacy), which does not count toward the three. I did not find a readable independent page with it.
The peace offer in Israel's declaration of independence: Avalon's text has it, but I found no second readable page, so I left it out of the facts.

Claims that Jewish forces took territory beyond the plan before 15 May appear on a UN Division for Palestinian Rights page, which counts as advocacy; I found no independent readable source and omitted it.
Khalidi's book is not cited (no authorised readable copy); his 2024 interview is used for the heard claim.
not_claimed: This card does not claim the UN vote made the 1948 war or the later displacement of Palestinians right, wrong or inevitable.
It does not claim the vote was free of great-power pressure or that Palestinian Arabs were consulted in the way they wanted.
It does not claim Jewish forces took only land the plan gave them; Israel ended up with more.
It does not say who fired first in the civil war that followed the vote.

answer_claims.says: The idea of splitting Palestine came first from a British commission in 1937.
Arab leaders rejected it; Jewish opinion was divided.
On 29 November 1947 the UN General Assembly recommended a Jewish state and an Arab state, by 33 votes to 13.
Palestinian Arab leaders rejected it; the Arab states in the Assembly voted against it, and Saudi Arabia said it did not consider itself bound.
Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948, and armies from Arab states entered Palestine on 15 May.
By the 1949 ceasefires Israel held more land than the plan had given it, about 78 percent of the former mandate.
The record shows a recommendation, one side that accepted it, one that rejected it, and a war.

skeptic.notes: Read two or more sources per fact; quotes are on the pages. Pro-Palestinian attack (the stronger one): the claim is 'imposed by outside powers'. The card gives the vote and the rejections but no fact on what the plan allotted against who lived and owned land there (about 56 percent to the Jewish state; population and land-ownership shares), nor on the fighting between November 1947 and 15 May 1948, nor on Jewish forces holding ground beyond the plan before the invasion. A reader cannot test 'imposed' or 'by force' from these facts. Pro-Israel attack: 'the Arab side rejected, the Jewish side accepted' is stated flatly, but Arab dissent is missing (Abdullah of Transjordan favoured partition in 1937 and dealt with the Jewish Agency in 1948 - not on the card), and the card does not say the Arab states' stated aim was to prevent partition. must-fix: fact 8 said '77 to 78 percent' and no cited page says 77; fixed to 'about 78'. must-fix (writer): add a sourced fact on the plan's shares and populations. should-fix: great-power pressure appears only as Khalidi's heard quote and a Saudi statement; add a fact if the answer is to address it. should-fix: fact 5 'Arab states ... refused to be bound' was carried by one government (Saudi Arabia); reworded to what the sources show, and the Israel Law Review line is a participant's 'better view', not a finding. should-fix: the 1937 Zionist Congress detail rests on the Jewish Virtual Library (advocacy) plus a Jerusalem Post piece citing Laqueur; added the 300-158 vote to contested. nit: Britannica pages could not be read live (archive quotes kept); fact 7 'invasion' wording is contested, now in contested. Independence: facts 0-4 draw on UN, EBSCO, Lumen, Britannica - separate publishers but reference works that follow the same standard narrative; no copying seen.
